summary: Maat is the order of the universe in the shape of a feather; Nut is the sky arched over her husband Geb, swallowing the sun every evening.
look: Maat is a seated or kneeling woman with one tall ostrich feather on her head; kings constantly offer a tiny figure of her to the gods. Nut is a long, star-covered woman bent over the world on fingertips and toes, painted across tomb ceilings and inside coffin lids. Geb lies beneath her, often green, sometimes with a goose on his head.
story:
The word maat meant the order set in place at creation: truth, justice, balance, the seasons turning and the sun rising. Her opposite was isfet, chaos. Kings claimed to 'live on Maat', put her in their names, and in countless temple scenes offer the gods a tiny squatting figure of her, a way of saying 'I have kept the world in order'. From the 5th Dynasty the vizier who ran justice was called 'Priest of Maat', and at the judgement of the dead the heart was weighed against her feather.

Nut was the sky, daughter of Shu, the air, and Tefnut, moisture. Unusually, the sky was female and the earth, her brother-husband Geb, male. Shu holds them apart. Each evening Nut swallows the sun, which travels through her body during the night and is born from her at dawn. Coffin lids were painted with her on the inside, so the dead lay in the sky's embrace, waiting to rise like the sun.

Plutarch tells how the sun forbade Nut to give birth on any day of the year. Thoth won five extra days by gambling with the moon, and on them she bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Seth, Isis and Nephthys: the five extra days at the end of the Egyptian calendar.
details: Watch for the king holding out a tiny crouching woman with a feather: he is offering Maat herself to the gods.
Tomb of Ramesses VI, KV9 (21st): two huge figures of Nut stretch back to back across the burial-chamber ceiling.
Inside coffin lids in the museums: Nut with outstretched arms or wings, embracing the dead person.
Throne names often contain her: Hatshepsut's Maatkare and Ramesses II's Usermaatre both include the Maat sign.
fun_fact: Egypt made the earth a man and the sky a woman, the reverse of most mythologies, including the Greek pair of Ouranos the sky and Gaia the earth.
narration: Three gods here hold the universe together. Maat is the woman with a single ostrich feather on her head. She is truth, justice and order, everything that keeps the sun rising and the river flooding. Her opposite was chaos. A king's first job was to uphold Maat, and on temple walls you will see him offering the gods a tiny crouching figure of her: proof that he kept the world in order. When you died, your heart was weighed against her feather. Nut is the sky, a long woman covered in stars, arched over the world on her fingertips and toes. Geb, the earth, lies beneath her, and their father Shu, the air, holds them apart. Unusually, the sky here is female and the earth male, the reverse of the Greek Ouranos and Gaia. Every evening Nut swallows the sun, and every dawn she gives birth to it again. That is why she is painted inside coffin lids: the dead lie in her arms, waiting to be reborn. In the tomb of Ramesses the Sixth, look up: Nut's body stretches across the whole ceiling.

period: Household gods, popular from the Middle Kingdom, c. 2000 BC, to the Roman period
summary: A grimacing dwarf and a pregnant hippo never got grand temples, but they guarded every Egyptian bedroom, birth and baby.
look: Bes is a bandy-legged dwarf with a lion's mane and ears, a feather crown and often his tongue out, and he faces you head-on, which almost no other Egyptian god does. Taweret stands upright: a pregnant hippo with human breasts, lion's paws and a crocodile's back and tail, often leaning on the sa sign of protection. Look for both on furniture, headrests, mirrors and amulets in museum cases, and for Bes dancing at Philae's Hathor temple.
story:
Egypt's great gods lived in temples ordinary people could not enter. At home, people relied on smaller, tougher protectors. Bes, possibly of Nubian origin, killed snakes, scared off demons, watched over children and stood by women in labour. His ugliness was the point: demons fled his face, and his music and dancing drove off evil. He appears on beds, headrests, mirror handles, feeding bottles and magic knives, and a painting at Deir el-Medina shows a musician with Bes tattooed on her thigh. Later he guarded the birth houses of Ptolemaic temples, and his cult spread to Phoenicia, Cyprus, Persia and Ibiza.

Taweret, 'the Great One', a polite name for a dangerous creature, was the female hippo, fiercest of mothers. Egyptians hunted male hippos as agents of chaos but honoured the female for defending her young. Hippo-goddess amulets go back to prehistory; from the Middle Kingdom Taweret appears on ivory birth wands and children's cups. Even at Amarna, where Akhenaten banned the old gods, people kept her image at home.

Do not confuse her with Ammit, the crocodile-lion-hippo 'devourer' who waits at the judgement of the dead.
details: Bes faces you directly while almost every other god is in profile: the stare is meant to frighten demons away.
Philae (18th): in the small Hathor temple, Bes plays instruments and dances for the goddess.
Edfu's birth house (20th): little figures of Bes squat on top of the columns above the capitals.
Taweret's crocodile tail runs down her back like a cape: look at her figurines from the side.
fun_fact: The Minoans of Crete borrowed Taweret: the lion-like 'Minoan Genius' carrying jugs on Cretan seals is widely thought to descend from her.
narration: The great gods lived in temples ordinary people could never enter. At home, Egyptians trusted two tougher, friendlier guards. Bes is the bandy-legged dwarf with a lion's mane, a crown of feathers and his tongue sticking out. Unlike almost every other god, he faces you head on, because his job was to stare demons down. He killed snakes, protected children, danced and played music to scare evil away, and stood beside women giving birth. You find him on beds, mirrors, headrests and baby bottles, and one painting shows a musician with Bes tattooed on her thigh. Taweret, whose name means the Great One, is a pregnant hippo standing on her hind legs, with lion's paws and a crocodile's back. Egyptians feared male hippos but admired the females, the fiercest mothers on the river. Even when Akhenaten banned the old gods, people kept Taweret at home. On Crete, the Minoans borrowed her too. At Edfu's birth house on the 20th, look at the tops of the columns: little figures of Bes squat there, grinning.

period: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, Amarna Period, c. 1353-1336 BC
summary: For some 17 years a pharaoh shut down Egypt's gods for a single sun disc, built a capital in the desert and changed art. Then it all vanished.
look: The Aten is a plain sun disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding ankhs to the noses of the royal family. Amarna art is easy to spot: long faces, full lips, narrow shoulders, wide hips, and tender family scenes. You will meet it in the Akhenaten colossi in the Cairo museums, on the back of Tutankhamun's golden throne at the GEM (11th) and in the talatat wall at the Luxor Museum (22nd).
story:
Amenhotep IV came to the throne around 1353 BC. The Aten, the 'disc' of the sun, had long been an aspect of Ra and was already honoured under his father, Amenhotep III. The new king went much further. In about his fifth year he became Akhenaten, 'effective spirit of the Aten', and began a capital on virgin ground in Middle Egypt: Akhetaten, 'Horizon of the Aten', today Amarna. Built mostly of whitewashed mud brick, it was largely finished within about four years, and boundary stelae marked its limits.

Aten temples were open to the sky, with no dark sanctuary and no cult statue. Only the king and Nefertiti, shown almost as his equal, could approach the god; everyone else worshipped through them. Amun's temples were closed and his name hacked out across Egypt. Whether this was the first monotheism or the worship of one god without denying the rest is still debated; the Great Hymn to the Aten is often compared with Psalm 104. Art changed overnight: elongated bodies, the king kissing his daughters, sunlight pouring over the family. Clay tablets found at Amarna in 1887, the Amarna letters, preserve the diplomatic mail of Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites and Canaan's rulers.

After Akhenaten's death the experiment collapsed. Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun and the court left Amarna; later kings pulled down the Aten temples and packed their small blocks, talatat, inside Karnak's pylons as fill. That is how thousands survived to be reassembled.
details: Sun disc with long rays ending in hands: the Aten. Only the royal family receives the ankhs held to their noses.
Tutankhamun's golden throne (GEM, 11th): the Aten shines on the young king and queen, a survivor of his Amarna childhood.
Luxor Museum (22nd): the talatat wall rebuilds an Aten temple scene from small blocks recovered inside a Karnak pylon.
Hacked-out and recut Amun figures on Luxor and Karnak walls are scars of this reign and its reversal.
fun_fact: Akhetaten was abandoned so quickly and completely that it is the only ancient Egyptian city whose street plan survives in detail.
narration: For about 17 years, one pharaoh tried to switch off Egypt's gods. Amenhotep the Fourth came to the throne around 1353 BC. Around his fifth year he renamed himself Akhenaten, effective spirit of the Aten, the sun disc, and moved the court to a brand new city on empty desert in Middle Egypt: Akhetaten, Horizon of the Aten, today called Amarna. It was thrown up in mud brick in about four years. The Aten was not a statue. It was sunlight itself, drawn as a disc whose rays end in little hands, holding the sign of life to the noses of the king and his wife Nefertiti. Only they could speak to the god, and everyone else worshipped through them. Amun's temples were closed and his name chiselled out across Egypt. Was it the first monotheism? Scholars still argue. Art changed overnight: long faces, wide hips, the king kissing his daughters in the sun. Then he died, and it all collapsed. His probable son Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun and brought Amun back, and later kings pulled the Aten temples down and stuffed their small stone blocks into the pylons at Karnak. That is why thousands survived. On the back of Tutankhamun's golden throne at the GEM, look for the sun disc with hands, shining on the young king and queen.

summary: Hieroglyphs are not picture-writing: most signs stand for sounds. Learn two dozen and you can start reading names off temple walls.
look: Hieroglyphs run in rows or columns, usually right to left, but the signs tell you: people, birds and animals face the beginning of the line, so read towards their faces. Signs on top are read before signs below. On this trip every wall is a text, and the bigger the carving, the more public the message.
story:
Writing appeared in Egypt around 3200 BC, among the earliest in the world and probably invented independently. In the classical Middle Kingdom about 900 signs were in use; Ptolemaic priests multiplied them to more than 5,000.

The system mixes three kinds of sign. Sound signs include 24 'alphabet' signs for single consonants, plus signs for two or three consonants. Word signs show the thing meant: a sun disc for 'sun'. Silent determinatives at the end of a word give its category: a seated man for a person, walking legs for movement, a papyrus roll for an abstract idea. Vowels were not written, which is why books disagree between Amun, Amon and Amen; Egyptologists insert a convenient 'e', so nfr becomes nefer.

For daily use scribes wrote fast cursive forms: hieratic, then from about 650 BC demotic. Coptic, written with Greek letters plus a few demotic signs, is the last stage of the language and still used in Coptic church services.

The last dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394. Greek and Roman writers then imagined the signs as mystical symbols, a belief that blocked decipherment for some 1,400 years. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Building on Thomas Young's work, Jean-François Champollion, who knew Coptic, showed in 1822 that the cartouches of Ptolemy and Cleopatra spelled sounds, and that the script was 'figurative, symbolic and phonetic all at once'.
details: Vulture = a (glottal stop), reed leaf = i, forearm = a (ayin), quail chick = w, foot = b, stool = p, horned viper = f, owl = m.
Water ripple = n, mouth = r, reed shelter = h, twisted flax = h, round placenta = kh, animal belly = kh, folded cloth = s.
Pool = sh, hill slope = q, basket with handle = k, jar stand = g, bread loaf = t, tethering rope = tj, hand = d, cobra = dj.
Which way? Read towards the faces of people, birds and animals, and take the top sign before the one below it.
fun_fact: 'Hieroglyph' is Greek for 'sacred carving', a fair translation of the Egyptians' own name for their script: 'the words of the god'.
narration: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, but most of them are sounds. That was the great discovery of 1822, and it means you can start reading. The system mixes three kinds of sign. Some spell sounds: there are 24 signs for single consonants, like an alphabet, plus signs for two or three consonants together. Some stand for whole words. And some are silent hints at the end of a word, telling you what kind of thing it is: a seated man for a person, walking legs for movement. Vowels were never written, which is why the same god is Amun, Amon or Amen in different books. Now the basics. An owl is m. Water, a zigzag line, is n. A mouth is r. A loaf of bread, a little half circle, is t. A foot is b, a quail chick is w, a horned viper is f, a folded cloth is s, a reed leaf is i, a hand is d. To know which way to read, look at the faces of the birds and people: you read towards them. For everyday writing, scribes used fast handwriting called hieratic and demotic. The last hieroglyphs ever carved are at Philae, dated 394 AD, and you will stand near them on the 18th. And a gift from Egypt to Greece: through the Phoenicians, these signs are distant ancestors of the Greek alphabet. On the next wall, find an owl and say m.

period: Cartouches used from the end of Dynasty 3, c. 2600 BC, to the Roman emperors
summary: The rope oval around a king's name is a game you can play on every wall: learn six cartouches and Ramesses, Tutankhamun and Hatshepsut will jump out.
look: A cartouche is a stretched oval of rope tied off with a bar at one end, enclosing a royal name; kings usually show two side by side. The first, introduced by a sedge plant and a bee, 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt', holds the throne name; the second, after a duck and a sun disc, 'Son of Ra', holds the birth name. Gods' names inside, like Ra's sun disc or Amun's name, are written first out of respect even when they are read later.
story:
A king had five names; the three outside cartouches (Horus, Two Ladies and Golden Horus names) rarely matter to visitors. The cartouche, Egyptian shenu, is a stretched shen ring, a loop of rope meaning eternity, wrapped protectively around the name. It appears at the end of the 3rd Dynasty and became standard under Sneferu.

The cheat sheet. Ramesses II's birth name, Ra-messu, is the sun disc, a sign like three fox skins tied together (ms), and folded-cloth s signs, usually with 'beloved of Amun'. His throne name, User-maat-Ra, is the sun disc, the goddess Maat with her feather and a jackal-headed staff (user, 'strong'). The Greek historian Diodorus rendered it 'Osymandyas', which became Shelley's Ozymandias.

Tutankhamun: Amun's name (reed leaf, game board, water ripple) on top for honour, then tut (loaf, quail chick, loaf), then the ankh. His throne name Neb-kheperu-Ra is sun, scarab and basket. Thutmose III's Men-kheper-Ra is sun, game board and scarab, stamped on scarab amulets for centuries after his death. Amenhotep III's Neb-maat-Ra is sun, Maat and basket. Hatshepsut's Maat-ka-Ra is sun, Maat and the raised arms of the ka. Khufu is placenta, quail chick, viper, quail chick: Kh-w-f-w.

The Ptolemies spelled Greek names letter by letter, which is how Champollion cracked the code: Ptolemy and Cleopatra share a stool (p), a lion (l) and a looped cord (o).
details: Sedge and bee before a cartouche: 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt', the throne name. Duck and sun: 'Son of Ra', the birth name.
Ramesses II: sun disc, three tied fox skins, folded cloths. Count them at Abu Simbel, Luxor and Karnak.
Tutankhamun: Amun's name on top, then loaf, chick, loaf, then the ankh. Check his coffins and throne at the GEM.
Hatshepsut's Maat-ka-Ra was often chiselled out after her death: look for battered or recut cartouches at her temple.
fun_fact: 'Cartouche' is French soldiers' slang: Napoleon's troops thought the ovals looked like the paper cartridges for their muskets.
narration: Every royal name in Egypt sits inside an oval loop of rope called a cartouche, and reading them is the best game you can play on this trip. The rope is a stretched shen ring, the sign of eternity, wrapped around the name to protect it. The word cartouche comes from Napoleon's soldiers, who thought it looked like a musket cartridge. Kings usually show two cartouches. The first, after a sedge plant and a bee, is the throne name. The second, after a duck and a sun disc meaning Son of Ra, is the birth name. Here is your cheat sheet. Ramesses: a sun disc, then a sign like three fox skins tied together, then folded cloths. His throne name, User maat Ra, has the sun, the goddess Maat with her feather and a jackal headed staff. The Greek historian Diodorus turned it into Osymandyas, Shelley's Ozymandias. Tutankhamun: the name of Amun on top, out of respect, then a loaf, a quail chick, a loaf, and finally the ankh. Thutmose the Third: a sun, a game board and a scarab. Hatshepsut: a sun, the goddess Maat and two raised arms. Gods' names go at the top even when you read them last. The Greek kings spelled their names sound by sound, so Ptolemy and Cleopatra share a stool for p, a lion for l and a loop for o. At Abu Simbel, hunt for the fox skins of Ramesses.

summary: A handful of signs repeat on every wall: life, stability, power, eternity, union. Learn them and the decoration starts to read like a sentence.
look: These signs appear in gods' hands, on thrones, in friezes along the tops and bottoms of walls, and as amulets in every museum case. The ankh is the looped cross; the djed a pillar with four crossbars; the was a long staff with a forked foot and an animal head; the shen a circle of rope sitting on a line.
story:
The ankh means life. The same consonants spelled 'mirror' and 'bouquet', so mirrors were made in its shape. Nobody agrees what object it began as: a sandal strap, a knot, even a bull's vertebra. Gods hold it to the king's nose to give him the breath of life, and chains of ankhs can stand for the water poured over him. Egypt's Christians adopted a looped cross, the crux ansata, and it survives in Coptic art.

The djed pillar means stability and was understood as Osiris's backbone; at festivals the king and priests hauled a djed upright with ropes. The was sceptre, a staff with a forked foot and the head of the Seth animal, means power; Thebes' own name, Waset, is written with it. Ptah's staff combines all three, and friezes repeat them above a basket sign: 'all life, power and stability'.

The shen, a loop of rope tied at the base, is eternity and the origin of the cartouche; falcons and vultures clutch it in their claws. The tyet, the 'Isis knot', means protection. Sema-tawy, 'uniting the Two Lands', is a windpipe-and-lungs sign around which the plant of the south and the papyrus of the north are knotted, by Nile gods or by Horus and Seth, on the sides of royal thrones. Under the king's feet you often find the Nine Bows, Egypt's traditional enemies, or bound prisoners, so he tramples them forever. On temple gateways he smites a bunch of foreigners held by the hair: a pose already on the Narmer Palette, about 5,000 years old.
details: Ankh held to the king's nose: a god giving him the breath of life. Common in Luxor and Abu Simbel reliefs.
Abu Simbel colossi (17th): on the throne sides, two Nile gods knot papyrus and lily around the sema-tawy sign.
Edfu (20th) and Philae (18th) pylons: the king grabs enemies by the hair and raises his mace, the smiting pose.
A flat basket under signs means 'all' or 'lord'; a falcon or vulture with spread wings usually grips a shen ring.
Statue bases and footstools: bows and bound captives under the king's feet, his enemies trampled forever.
fun_fact: When Christians tore down Alexandria's Serapeum in 391, they found ankh-like signs on its stones; pagans said they meant 'life to come', and the Christians claimed them as crosses.
narration: A few signs appear on almost every wall in Egypt, and once you know them, the decoration starts to read like a sentence. The ankh, the cross with a loop on top, means life. Watch the gods hold it to the king's nose: they are giving him the breath of life. The djed, a pillar with four crossbars, means stability, and was thought of as the backbone of Osiris. The was sceptre, a tall staff with a forked foot and an animal's head, means power. Ptah holds all three in one staff, and temple friezes repeat them in rows: all life, power and stability. The shen, a circle of rope tied at the bottom, means eternity. Stretch it long and you get the cartouche around a king's name. The tyet, like an ankh with drooping arms, is the knot of Isis, for protection. On the sides of royal thrones, look for two figures tying a papyrus and a lily around a windpipe and lungs. That is sema tawy, the union of the Two Lands, south and north. On temple gateways the king grabs a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his mace. That pose goes back 5,000 years, to the Narmer Palette. Under his feet there are often bows or bound prisoners, so he tramples his enemies forever. At Abu Simbel on the 17th, look at the side of a colossus's throne: two Nile gods are tying the knot of union.

period: Wedjat amulets from the late Old Kingdom, scarabs common from c. 2000 BC, both into Roman times
summary: The eye Seth tore out and Thoth healed, and the dung beetle that rolls the sun: Egypt's two favourite lucky charms, made by the million.
look: The wedjat is a stylised eye with an eyebrow, a line dropping below it and a curl, like the markings on a falcon's cheek. The scarab is a beetle carved in stone or moulded in blue-green faience, its flat underside carrying a name or motto. Museum cases hold hundreds of both, and on Tutankhamun's pectorals at the GEM the scarab often has wings and pushes up a sun.
story:
In the myth Seth tore out Horus's eye, or smashed it to pieces; Thoth, or in another version Hathor with gazelle's milk, restored it. From the New Kingdom it was called the wedjat, 'the whole one'. Horus offered his healed eye to his dead father Osiris, so the eye came to stand for every offering, and its return to wholeness for the waxing moon. It was among the most popular amulets for over 2,000 years; embalmers often laid one over the incision through which the organs were removed. Painted on coffins it let the dead look out, and on boats' bows it let the ship see. A long-popular theory reads the parts of the eye as fractions from 1/2 to 1/64, but it is now challenged, and the claim that the pharmacist's Rx comes from the eye is a modern myth.

The scarab, Egyptian kheper, means 'to come into being'. Egyptians watched the dung beetle roll its ball and saw Khepri rolling the sun into the sky each morning. Scarab amulets became hugely popular around 2000 BC; their flat bases carried names, mottos and designs and worked as seals, and Men-kheper-Ra, Thutmose III's throne name, is the commonest royal name on them. Amenhotep III issued large scarabs like press releases, announcing his marriage to Tiye and his lion hunts. Heart scarabs, large dark stones placed on the mummy, carried Book of the Dead spell 30B, begging the heart not to testify against its owner at the judgement.
details: Middle Kingdom coffins have a pair of eyes painted near the head, so the dead could look out towards the sunrise.
Winged scarabs pushing a sun disc on Tutankhamun's pectorals at the GEM: Khepri bringing the dawn.
Karnak (22nd): Amenhotep III's giant granite scarab stands by the Sacred Lake; visitors walk round it for luck.
Heart scarabs: large, dark green or black stone beetles, the flat base covered in lines of text.
fun_fact: Glass eye beads strung with wedjat amulets from the 13th century BC may be distant ancestors of the blue evil-eye bead, the Greek mati.
narration: These are Egypt's two favourite lucky charms, made by the million. The Eye of Horus is a painted eye with an eyebrow, a line dropping down below it and a curl, like the markings on a falcon's cheek. In the myth, Seth tore out Horus's eye and broke it, and Thoth, the god of wisdom, healed it. Its name, wedjat, means the whole one, the eye made sound again. Horus gave it to his dead father Osiris to bring him back to life, so the eye became a symbol of every offering, and of healing and protection. Embalmers placed one over the cut where they had removed the organs, and Egyptians painted eyes on coffins and on the prows of boats, so they could see where they were going. The scarab is a dung beetle. Egyptians watched it roll a ball of dung and saw the god Khepri rolling the sun up into the sky each morning. His name means coming into being. Scarab amulets were carved with names and used as seals. Amenhotep the Third even sent out large scarabs like press releases, announcing his marriage and his lion hunts. A big stone heart scarab, laid on the mummy, carried a spell begging the heart not to tell tales at the final judgement. At Karnak on the 22nd, find the giant stone scarab by the Sacred Lake. Everyone walks around it for luck.

summary: White for the south, red for the north, both together for all Egypt: a king's crown tells you what he claims and what he is doing.
look: Check the king's head first. A tall white bowling-pin crown is the south; a flat red crown with a tall back spike and a curly wire is the north; one inside the other is the double crown. The striped headcloth is the nemes, the blue helmet dotted with small discs is the khepresh, and the cobra at the brow is the uraeus. You will see them all on Tutankhamun's treasures at the GEM and on every Luxor wall.
story:
The white crown, hedjet, belonged to Upper Egypt, the south; the red crown, deshret, to Lower Egypt, the Delta. Combined they made the double crown, which the Greeks called pschent, from the Egyptian for 'the two powerful ones'. No red or white crown has ever been found, so we know them only from images.

The nemes, a striped linen headcloth gathered into a tail at the back, is the one on Tutankhamun's mask and the Sphinx. The blue crown, khepresh, studded with small discs, is typical of the New Kingdom and often worn in battle scenes. Gods have their own headgear: Osiris's atef, a white crown with feathers; Amun's two tall plumes. Queens wear the vulture cap, wings folded around the head.

At the king's brow rears the uraeus, the cobra goddess Wadjet of the north, said to spit fire at his enemies; on Tutankhamun's mask she rises beside the vulture Nekhbet of the south, together the 'Two Ladies'. Add a false beard, straight and squared for the living king, long, braided and curled at the tip for gods and the dead, the crook and flail, and a bull's tail hanging from the kilt. The Kushite kings of Dynasty 25 wore a close cap with two cobras.
details: Tutankhamun's gold mask (GEM, 11th): nemes headcloth, vulture and cobra side by side at the brow, braided divine beard.
Battle and procession scenes at Abu Simbel and Karnak: look for the blue khepresh with its small gold discs.
Statues' jaws: thin raised lines running up to the ears are the straps that held the false beard on.
Queens and goddesses: vulture cap, often topped with Hathor's horns and disc or two tall plumes, as Nefertari wears at Abu Simbel.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun's mummy wore a beaded linen skullcap decorated with four cobras bearing the name of the Aten, a souvenir of his Amarna childhood.
narration: Before you look at a king's face, look at his hat. It tells you what he claims. The tall white crown, shaped like a bowling pin, is Upper Egypt, the south. The flat red crown with a tall spike at the back and a curly wire in front is Lower Egypt, the north. Put one inside the other and you have the double crown: all of Egypt. No real one has ever been found, so we only know them from pictures. The striped linen headcloth is the nemes, the one on Tutankhamun's gold mask and on the Sphinx. The blue helmet dotted with little discs is the khepresh, often worn in battle scenes. At the brow rises the uraeus, a cobra goddess who spits fire at the king's enemies. On Tutankhamun's mask she has a vulture beside her, the protector of the south. Then the false beard: straight for a living king, curled at the tip for gods and the dead. It was tied on with straps, and even Hatshepsut wore one. On the gold mask at the GEM, find the cobra and the vulture side by side on the forehead.
